definition: Specified bound on the value of a functional indicator or condition indicator used to assess the ability of a structure, system or component to meet its design and safety requirements
An airtight door system that preserves the pressure integrity of the containment structure of a nuclear reactor, while allowing access to personnel and equipment.
The process of making a radioisotope by bombarding a stable element with neutrons or protons.
The same as the Fuel Core Assembly
The end-to-end dimension of fuel material within a fuel assembly (also known as a "fuel bundle" or "fuel element").

The rate of disintegration (transformation) or decay of radioactive material per unit time. The units of activity (also known as radioactivity) are the curie (Ci) and the becquerel (Bq). For related information, see Measuring Radiation.
is the adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or dissolved solid to a surface.

Reactors that differ from today’s reactors primarily by their use of inert gases, molten salt mixtures, or liquid metals to cool the reactor core. Advanced reactors can also consider fuel materials and designs that differ radically from today’s enriched-uranium-dioxide pellets within zirconium cladding.
A U.S. State that has signed an agreement with the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) authorizing the State to regulate certain uses of radioactive materials within the State.
The collection of samples of air to measure the radioactivity or to detect the presence of radioactive material, particulate matter, or chemical pollutants in the air.

As defined in Title 10, Section 20.1003, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR 20.1003), the airborne radioactivity area is a room, enclosure, or area in which airborne radioactive materials, composed wholly or partially of licensed material, exist in concentrations that 
(1) exceed the derived air concentration limits (DACs), or 
(2) would result in an individual present in the area without respiratory protection exceeding, during those hours, 0.6 percent of the annual limit on intake (ALI) or 12 DAC-hours.
A type of uncertainty that is irreducible.

ASR is a chemical combining of reactive silica from the concrete aggregate with the alkali from the cement paste in the presence of moisture. The result of the reaction is a gel, which can expand and may cause micro-cracks in the concrete.
A declaration, statement, or assertion of impropriety or inadequacy associated with NRC-regulated activities, the validity of which has not been established.

A positively charged particle ejected spontaneously from the nuclei of some radioactive elements. It is identical to a helium nucleus that has a mass number of 4 and an electrostatic charge of +2. It has low penetrating power and a short range (a few centimeters in air). The most energetic alpha particle will generally fail to penetrate the dead layers of cells covering the skin, and can be easily stopped by a sheet of paper. Alpha particles are hazardous when an alpha-emitting isotope is inside the body.

word: American Society for Testing and Materials

definition: An operational process deviating from normal operation that is expected to occur once or several times during the operating lifetime of the Nuclear Plant but that – in view of the appropriate design provisions – does not cause significant damage to items important to safety or lead to accident conditions

as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) A principle of radiation protection that holds that exposures to radiation are kept as low as reasonably achievable, social and economic factors taken into account.

The energy that is released through a nuclear reaction or radioactive decay process. One kind of nuclear reaction is fission, which occurs in a nuclear reactor and releases energy, usually in the form of heat and radiation. In a nuclear power plant, this heat is used to boil water to produce steam that can be used to drive large turbines. The turbines drive generators to produce electrical power.
The expected fraction of time, during a calendar year, that the NHSS is capable of producing net energy output.
Fuel thermomechanical and release modelling framework

The basis explains why a requirement exists and why it has been specified in a particular manner or at a particular value during the engineering design process. Basis information is delineated in design input information, design constraints, and intermediate outputs, such as design studies, analyses, and calculations.
An accident less frequent than a design basis accident (,<10-5). A beyond design basis accident may or may not involve core degradation

word: Canadian Standards Association of Nuclear Operators

definition: Canadian regulations define this as a nuclear substance listed in column 1 of Schedule 1 that is in the corresponding form set out in column 2 and the corresponding quantity set out in column 4 of Schedule 1 (Source: Nuclear Security Regulations)
A subcritical reactor state with a defined margin to prevent a return to criticality without external action at a reactor outlet temperature below ,350°C
The primary coolant inventory is reduced to slightly sub-atmospheric (approximately -0.5 psig) pressure.

Accident conditions for which a reactor facility is designed according to established design criteria, and for which damage to the fuel and the release of radioactive material are kept within authorized limits

design-basis earthquake (DBE) As defined in the CSA Group publication CSA N289.1-08, General requirements for seismic design and qualification of CANDU nuclear power plants, referenced in the nuclear power plant licence: an engineering representation of potentially severe effects at the site due to earthquake ground motions having a selected probability of exceedance of 1x10-4 per year, or such probability level as determined by the regulatory authority.
The characteristics of a potential adversary in respect of which counter meass are incorporated into the design and evaluation of a physical protection system.

Requirements for information and/or confirmation of technical characteristics specified by designers. Design Data Needs are the basis for establishing the scope of the supporting technology development program.

A subset of beyond-design-basis accidents that are considered in the design process of the facility in accordance with best-estimate methodology to keep releases of radioactive material within acceptable limits. Design extension conditions could include severe accident conditions

A response spectrum is a plot of the peak or steady-state response of a series of oscillators of varying natural frequency, that are forced into motion by the same base vibration or shock.The resulting plot can then be used to pick off the response of any linear system, given its natural frequency of oscillation.
The nominal value of a plant or system operating parameter, plus an appropriate margin.
This is equal to one year of operation at 100% rated power for a plant operating equivalent availability of ,95%.

emergency planning zone The offsite area around a facility for which emergency planning and preparation are done in advance, to ensure that necessary and effective protective actions can be taken to protect the public, property or the environment in case of an accident.
environmental assessment (EA) An assessment of the environmental effects of a project.

equipment qualification The process for certifying equipment as having satisfied the requirements for operability under conditions relevant to its safety functions. Equipment qualification includes the generation and maintenance of evidence to ensure that equipment will operate on demand, under specified service conditions, to meet system performance requirements.

is state-of-the-art HTGR fuel that ensures containment of radioactive materials during operations and accident conditions. The fuel is manufactured with TRISO coated fuel particles that retain fission products. The TRISO coated fuel particles are bonded together in a SiC matrix to form FCM™ fuel pellets.
Failure mode effects and criticality analysis
Refers to the time integrated flux of fast neutrons on a global or localized basis
Refers to heavy metal isotopes which are readily fissionable by neutrons at thermal energy (E ,< 2.8 eV), such as U-235, U-233, and Pu-239.
The assembly of all fuel containing elements.
A statement of what is to be achieved.

A systems engineering technique or method used to develop (1) functions required to meet established goals, (2) the relationship between functions and related requirements, and (3) the basis and justification for design selections through which the prescribed goals are met.

A reactor state where the reactor remains in a stable, sub-critical state, independent of any perturbation in reactivity produced by any change in core configuration, core properties, or process system failure and the safe maintenance activities can be performed
High Confidence of Low Probability of Failure

definition: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
Initial Public Offer which precedes a Public Listing

An event that initiates a sequence of events that could lead to a severe accident in the absence of action by a system important to safety, or an event involving a system important to safety that initiates a sequence of events that could have led to a severe accident if other systems important to safety had not functioned.
Kraftwerk Kennzeichen System (German for Power Plant Classification System)
Kerntechnischer Ausschuss (German Nuclear Safety Standards Commission)

A licence to construct a Class I nuclear facility : A document issued by Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission permitting the construction of a Class I nuclear facility after receipt and consideration of an application prepared in accordance with the requirements of SOR/2000-204 Class I Nuclear Facilities Regulations and RD/GD-369 Licence Application Guide Licence to Construct a Nuclear Power Plant

A licence to operate a Class I nuclear facility : A document issued by Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission permitting the operation of a Class I nuclear facility after submission and consideration of an application prepared in accordance with the requirements of SOR/2000-204 Class I Nuclear Facilities Regulations and REGDOC-1.1.3: Licence Application Guide: Licence to Operate a Nuclear Power Plant
Loss of helium circulation through the core by the Helium Circulator
Enriched uranium containing less than 20 percent by weight of isotope uranium-235, uranium-233, or combined uranium-233 and uranium-235.
Radioactive solid waste that contains material with radionuclide content above established clearance levels and exemption quantities, but that generally has limited amounts of long-lived activity.
Micro Modular Reactor Remote Power Plant
The reactor conditions characterized by cold shutdown, and the primary coolant is reduced to a depressurized operation with core inlet temperature less than ,250°F.
Treaty on the Non-proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
Expected mean value of a parameter at middle of cycle and middle of life operation for an average plant.

is the nuclear power plant that consists of a number High Temperature Gas-cooled Reactors (HTGR). These reactors supply heat. The Nuclear Plant includes all the equipment required to transport the heat from the reactor, support the operation of the plant and ensure the nuclear safety of the facility.
Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development
Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development
That earthquake which could reasonably be expected to affect the plant site during the operating life of the plant.
The calendar time from receipt of the operating license to completion of plant energy production.

A set of rules setting forth parameter limits and the functional capability and performance levels of equipment and personnel, which are approved by the regulatory body for safe operation of an authorized facility. This set of limits and conditions is monitored by or on behalf of the operator and can be controlled by the operator

the earthquake ground motion for which those features of the nuclear power plant necessary for continued operations without undue risk to health and safety of the public will remain functional. N289.1-08 ,General requirements for seismic design and qualification of CANDU nuclear power plants

A component whose functioning does not depend on an external input such as actuation, mechanical movement or supply of power. A passive component has no moving part, and, for example, only experiences a change in pressure, in temperature or in fluid flow in performing its functions. IAEA SAFETY GLOSSARY, 2016

All systems, structures and components that together accomplish the process of energy production, conversion and delivery, and support the human activities of administration, operation and maintenance.
The calendar time from the operating license issuance to completion of plant energy production.
The operational condition of the physical plant (or module) at a particular time and place, as described by an appropriate set of parameters.
A reactor shutdown in which the Reactor Protection System or operator action simultaneously inserts control materials and de-energizes the helium circulator to ensure reactor shutdown
Provision of alternative (identical or diverse) structures, systems and components, so that any one can perform the required function regardless of the state of operation or failure of any other
An observable and/or quantifiable bound on an attribute of the plant design or on the process by which the design is developed. See also Functional Requirement.
That earthquake for which those structures, systems, and components required to meet regulatory release limits are designed to remain functional with a high degree of confidence.
A state characterized by subcriticality of the reactor in which the fundamental safety functions can be ensured and maintained stable for a long time

a consistent and clearly defined method for classifying the safety significance of SSCs important to safety based on:
1. safety function(s) to be performed
2. consequence(s) of failure
3. probability that the SSC will be called upon to perform the safety function
4. the time following a PIE at which the SSC will be called upon to operate, and the expected duration of that operation

A margin to a value of safety variable for a barrier or a system at which damage or loss would occur. Safety margins are considered for those systems and barriers whose failure could potentially contribute to radiological releases

Identifier associated with systems, structures and components to denote that such are relied on during Design Basis Events to meet the regulatory offsite dose requirements and are subject to the quality requirements of NQA-1. The term
The sudden shutting down of a nuclear reactor, usually by rapid insertion of control rods, either automatically or manually by the reactor operator. Also known as a "reactor trip".

This is the length of time for which a system, a subsystem, or component shall be designed to perform within its performance requirements.Within this period of time, parts can be replaced so long as the system, subsystem, or components' availability requirements are met.

The instantaneous amount of reactivity by which the reactor is subcritical or would be subcritical from its present condition assuming all full-length rod banks (shutdown and control) are fully inserted except for the two shutdown rods of highest reactivity worth that is assumed to be fully withdrawn in consideration of single failure and possible maintenance, testing, inspection or repair.
A failure that results in the loss of capability of a component in a system to perform its intended safety function(s), and any resulting consequential failure(s)

General requirements for seismic design and qualification of CANDU nuclear power plants : Site design earthquake (SDE) — an engineering representation of the effects at the site of a set of possible earthquakes with an occurrence rate, based on historical records, not greater than 1 × 10–2 per year.

General requirements for seismic design and qualification of CANDU nuclear power plants : Site operating earthquake (SOE) — an engineering representation of ground motion established using the best estimate of the 1 × 10–2 seismic hazard ground motions.
A grouping of electrical, mechanical and/or structural components and associated software and human actions treated as a unit for technical, administrative or contractual purposes.
To be Confirmed and Subject to Change
A meas of the reactivity change due to changes in fuel and graphite temperature, expressed as Δk/°C.
Refers to the time-integrated flux of thermalized, or moderated neutrons, with energies below 2.38 eV.
a material in a nuclear reactor that absorbs neutrons without reproducing them a material that absorbs radiation or causes it to lose energy

is a power plant that generates power from the heat supplied by the Nuclear Plant and contains all the equipment to generate and supply power. The Adjacent Plant can also supply process heat to customer applications.
A material which adsorbs, especially a solid material, such as activated carbon, that has a high surface area and is used to capture a gas or liquid.
The fraction of time that a component or system is able to function. Availability can also mean the probability that a component or system will be able to function at any given time.
The fraction of time for which a system is capable of fulfilling its intended purpose.

fuel burnup The induced nuclear transformation of atoms during reactor operation, usually measd as energy generated in the fuel during its residence in the reactor core per unit mass of fuel (such as gigawatt-days per tonne of uranium). Also called burnup.
extremely harmful or that causes great damage or change.
the simultaneous production of electricity and heat, both of which are used.

common-cause failure (CCF) A failure of two or more structures, systems, or components due to a single specific event or cause, such as a natural phenomenon (earthquake, tornado, flood, etc.), design deficiency, manufacturing flaw, operation and maintenance error, human-induced destructive event, or aging effect.
Failure of two or more structures, systems and components due to a single specific event or cause
Methods or physical structures designed to prevent or control the release and the dispersion of radioactive substances.

contamination
1. Radioactive substances on surfaces, or within solids, liquids or gases (including the human body), where their presence is unintended or undesirable, or the process giving rise to their presence in such places.
2. The presence of a radioactive substance on a surface in quantities in excess of 0.4 Bq/cm2 for beta and gamma emitters and low toxicity alpha emitters, or 0.04 Bq/cm2 for all other alpha emitters.

1. A hierarchical deployment of different levels of diverse equipment and procedures to prevent the escalation of anticipated operational occurrences and to maintain the effectiveness of physical barriers placed between a radiation source or radioactive material and workers, members of the public or the environment, in operational states and, for some barriers, in accident conditions
2. The application of more than one protective meas for a given safety objective, such that the objective is achieved even if one of the protective meass fails.

Defence in depth A hierarchical deployment of different levels of diverse equipment and procedures to prevent the escalation of anticipated operational occurrences and to maintain the effectiveness of physical barriers placed between a radiation source or radioactive material and workers, members of the public or the environment, in operational states and, for some barriers, in accident conditions.

design envelope The range of conditions and events (including design extension conditions) that are explicitly taken into account in the design of a nuclear facility, such that significant radioactive releases would be practically eliminated by the planned operation of process and control systems, safety systems, safety support systems and complementary design features.

(under CEAA 2012) An assessment of the environmental effects of a designated project that is conducted in accordance with ,the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, 2012. (Source: CEAA 2012) Practitioners Glossary for the Environmental Assessment of Designated Projects Under the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, 2012 : An ,environmental assessment (EA) under CEAA 2012 predicts the environmental effects of a designated project, identified mitigation meass, assesses whether the designated project is likely to cause significant adverse environmental effects taking into account identified mitigation meass, and ensures a follow-up program is designated to verify the accuracy of the EA of the designated project and effectiveness of any mitigation meass”.

under the NSCA A technical assessment by CNSC staff of information required under the NSCA and the regulations made under the NSCA to inform and support the Commission’s determination on whether the applicant or licensee will make adequate provision for the protection of the environment and the health and safety of persons while carrying on a licensed activity.
Generation and maintenance of evidence to ensure that equipment will operate on demand, under specified service conditions, to meet system performance requirements
centimeter-gram-second unit of work or energy
exclusion zone A parcel of land within or surrounding a nuclear facility on which there is no permanent dwelling and over which a licensee has the legal authority to exercise control.
Capable of undergoing fission by interaction with slow neutrons.

guaranteed shutdown state (GSS) A reactor state with sufficient negative reactivity to ensure subcriticality in the event of any process failure and for which administrative safeguards (that is, reactor shutdown guarantees), approved by the senior operations authority and with which the CNSC concurs, are in place to prevent net removal of negative reactivity.
Safety achieved by the elimination of a specified hazard by means of the choice of material and design concept IAEA- TECDOC- 626; Sept 1991.
An identified event that leads to anticipated operational occurrences or accident conditions
Operation of a nuclear power plant within specified operational limits and conditions including startup, power operation, shutting down, shutdown, maintenance and testing.
A component that functions without depending on an external input such as actuation, mechanical movement or supply of power.

A configuration of reactor facility components, including the physical and thermodynamic states of the materials and the process fluids in them. Note: With respect to reactor facility design, a plant is said to be in one of the following states: normal operation, anticipated operational occurrence, design-basis accident, or beyond-design-basis accident (severe accidents and design extension conditions are a subset of the beyond-design-basis state),

Actions that detect, preclude or mitigate degradation of a functional structure, system or component to sustain or extend its useful life by controlling degradation and failures to an acceptable level

Preventive maintenance (or preventative maintenance) is planned maintenance that is regularly performed on a piece of equipment to lessen the likelihood of it failing. It is performed while the equipment is still working so that it does not break down unexpectedly.

reliability The ability of a structure, system or component to perform, in accordance with its defined specifications, its required function under given conditions for a defined time period or upon demand.
The probability that a system or component will meet its minimum performance requirements when called upon to do so.

safety analysis A systematic evaluation of the potential hazards that is associated with the conduct of a proposed activity or facility and that considers the effectiveness of preventive meass and strategies in reducing the effects of such hazards.

Analysis by means of appropriate analytical tools that establishes and confirms the design basis for the items important to safety; and ensures that the overall reactor facility design is capable of meeting the acceptance criteria for each plant state.
Evaluation of the potential hazards associated with the sconduct of an activity.
safety assessment An assessment of all aspects relevant to safety of the siting, design, construction, commissioning, operation or decommissioning of a nuclear facility

1. Assessment of all aspects of a practice that are relevant to protection and safety; for an authorized facility, this includes siting, design and operation of the facility.
2. Analysis to predict the performance of an overall system and its impact, where the performance meas is the radiological impact or some other global meas of the impact on safety.
3. The systematic process that is carried out throughout the design process to ensure that all the relevant safety requirements are met by the proposed (or actual) design. Safety assessment includes, but is not limited to, the formal safety analysis.
For nuclear power plants, the assignment to a limited number of safety classes of systems and components and other items of equipment on the basis of their functions and their safety significance

safety culture The characteristics of a work environment, such as values, rules and common understandings, that influence employee perceptions and attitudes about the importance that the organization places on safety.
The period from initial operation to final withdrawal from service of a structure, system or component.
A failure that results in the loss of capability of a component to perform its intended function(s), and any consequential failure(s) resulting from that single failure.
